analysis.one_liner: Bans the manufacture, use, and sale of commercial asbestos, with limited exemptions.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in September 2025 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, where no further action has been taken.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend the Toxic Substances Control Act to immediately prohibit making, processing, using, or selling commercial asbestos and any products containing it. Existing chlor-alkali facilities — which use asbestos to make chlorine — would get until January 1, 2030 to keep using it. The President could grant time-limited exemptions where asbestos is needed for national security and no alternative exists.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers in construction, manufacturing, shipyards, and auto repair, along with the general public, gain protection from asbestos exposure, which causes mesothelioma, lung cancer, and other fatal diseases. Future exposure from imported products and domestic processing would be cut off at the source.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers and the public exposed to asbestos

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits any person from manufacturing, processing, using, or distributing in commerce commercial asbestos or any mixture or article containing it, effective on enactment.
It covers all recognized commercial asbestos fiber types, including chrysotile, the only form still imported into the United States in significant quantities.

It closes off ongoing exposure through imported asbestos-containing products while allowing safe disposal of asbestos already installed in buildings, and exempting trace asbestos present only as an impurity.
Existing chlor-alkali plants get a transition period until January 1, 2030 to convert to non-asbestos technology rather than an abrupt cutoff.

analysis.who_pays: A small number of chlor-alkali facilities that still use asbestos diaphragms would bear conversion costs, though they get four-plus years to switch to alternatives. Companies that import or sell asbestos-containing products would lose that supply line.
analysis.who_pays_short: Chlor-alkali plants and asbestos product importers

drawbacks.text: The bill does not end all asbestos use immediately: chlor-alkali facilities in operation at enactment may keep using and processing commercial asbestos for diaphragms until January 1, 2030, prolonging exposure for plant workers during the transition.

Converting chlor-alkali plants to asbestos-free membrane technology imposes real capital costs on those facilities, costs that could be passed on in the price of chlorine and related chemical products.

The national security exemption, extendable once for up to three additional years (six years total), could keep limited asbestos use going for an extended period if a President finds no feasible alternative.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health benefit — eliminating a known cause of fatal cancers from commercial use — is large and permanent, while the costs fall on a small industry with a multi-year transition runway and a narrower product universe than older bans faced. The main honest criticism is the long chlor-alkali carve-out, which means workers in those plants continue facing asbestos exposure for years after enactment.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on September 16, 2025 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which has taken no action on it since.

narrative.text: Representative Suzanne Bonamici introduced the bill on September 16, 2025, joined by Representative Don Bacon.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce on the day of introduction.
No further action — no hearings, markup, or floor vote — appears in the action history as of the provided record.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For now, the status quo holds: companies that make or import asbestos-containing products, and chlor-alkali plants that use asbestos, continue operating under current rules with no new restrictions on the horizon.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Asbestos users and importers, for now

for.name: Rep. Suzanne Bonamici
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to committee.

for.name: Rep. Don Bacon
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor at introduction, giving the bill bipartisan sponsorship.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship is bipartisan — a Democratic sponsor from Oregon and a single Republican cosponsor from Nebraska — though the bill has no committee or floor action to judge broader support.

industries.note: These plants use asbestos to make chlorine and would lose that raw material entirely, but the bill lets existing facilities keep using it until January 1, 2030 to convert to asbestos-free membrane technology. For plant workers, the carve-out means continued asbestos exposure during the transition.

industries.industry: Importers and sellers of asbestos-containing products (brake pads, gaskets, friction products)
industries.note: The bill cuts off their supply chain by banning distribution in commerce of products containing commercial asbestos. Their profit depends on continuing to sell a material linked to fatal cancers, so their interest runs against the public's.

Banning new commercial use while preserving rules for compliant disposal of existing asbestos keeps demand for licensed removal work, and fewer new asbestos installations over time means less hazardous material in buildings.
Conversion costs could nudge up chlorine prices, but a full ban ends the risk of asbestos-related supply disruptions tied to a single hazardous input.

analysis.trajectory: Bills at this stage — referred to committee with minimal cosponsorship and no scheduled action — rarely reach the floor. Versions of an asbestos ban have been introduced repeatedly in past Congresses without becoming law, and with no committee action in the months since referral, this bill would need substantially more support to move before this Congress ends in January 2027.
